questions.stem: In August 1914 the Social Democrats (SPD) voted for war credits and the parties agreed to suspend political conflict. This truce was known as the:
options: Gleichschaltung
Burgfrieden
Kulturkampf
Weltpolitik
questions.explanation: The Burgfrieden ('castle peace') united Germans behind a war presented as defensive. The Kulturkampf was Bismarck's struggle with the Catholic Church, Weltpolitik was the Kaiser's pre-war 'world policy', and Gleichschaltung was the Nazi coordination of 1933.

questions.stem: The 'Turnip Winter' of 1916-17 in Germany was caused mainly by:
options: the government's decision to export food to Austria
the British blockade and a failed potato harvest
French occupation of Germany's main farming regions
a general strike by farm workers demanding peace
questions.explanation: The blockade cut imports of food and fertiliser, and a poor potato crop left many Germans living on turnips. Hunger and rising deaths among civilians weakened morale and fuelled later unrest.

questions.stem: From 1916 Field Marshal Hindenburg and General Ludendorff, at the head of the Third Supreme Command, increasingly controlled German policy. Historians have described this as a:
options: 'silent dictatorship', with the army overshadowing Kaiser and Reichstag
parliamentary government in which the Reichstag chose the army commanders
socialist government formed by an alliance of the SPD and trade unions
royal absolutism in which the Kaiser personally directed every battle
questions.explanation: The generals shaped war production, labour policy and war aims, and forced out a chancellor in 1917. The term 'silent dictatorship' captures how military leaders came to dominate civilian government.

questions.stem: In 1917 the Social Democrats split, and the Independent Social Democrats (USPD) were formed. The main cause was:
options: opposition to the Treaty of Versailles terms
disagreement over continuing to support the war
a dispute over women's right to vote after the war
the SPD leaders' decision to join the Nazi Party
questions.explanation: A growing minority opposed voting further war credits and broke away. The split in the left, deepened in 1918-19 by the founding of the Communist Party, shaped politics throughout the Weimar years. Versailles came only in 1919.

questions.stem: In late September 1918 Ludendorff told the Kaiser that Germany must seek an armistice and that a government based on the Reichstag majority should be formed. Historians often see his motive as:
options: a plan to continue the war with the help of new American allies
a response to the Allied occupation of Berlin earlier that month
shifting blame for defeat from the army onto the civilian politicians
a sincere conversion to democracy after reading Wilson's Fourteen Points
questions.explanation: With the army near collapse after the Allied offensives from August 1918, Ludendorff wanted the parliamentary parties to take responsibility for asking for peace. This laid the ground for the later stab-in-the-back myth. No Allied troops had reached Berlin.

questions.stem: In early November 1918 the German revolution began when:
options: Hitler's followers seized government buildings in Munich and Berlin
French troops entered Berlin and arrested the Kaiser and his generals
the Reichstag voted to end the monarchy after a national referendum
sailors at Kiel mutinied rather than sail on a last attack
questions.explanation: The naval mutiny spread as workers' and soldiers' councils formed in city after city. On 9 November the Kaiser's abdication was announced and the SPD's Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic from the Reichstag building.

questions.stem: On 10 November 1918 the new SPD leader Friedrich Ebert agreed with General Groener that the army would support his government. In return Ebert:
options: promised to restore the Kaiser once the war with the Allies ended
handed control of foreign policy to the Supreme Army Command
promised to keep order and resist a radical left-wing revolution
agreed to give the army a veto over the terms of the peace treaty
questions.explanation: The Ebert-Groener pact kept the old officer corps in place in exchange for its help against the far left. Critics argue it left the republic dependent on an army that did not share its values, as the use of the Freikorps in 1919 showed.

questions.stem: Why did the 'stab-in-the-back' myth, spread by Hindenburg and others after 1918, damage the new republic?
options: It branded the politicians who made peace as traitors, the 'November criminals'
It proved that the Kaiser had lost the war, so monarchists supported the republic
It led the Allies to cancel reparations because Germany had not really been beaten
It persuaded the army to hand all its weapons to the workers' councils in 1919
questions.explanation: The myth claimed the unbeaten army had been betrayed at home by socialists, Jews and politicians, although the generals themselves had sought the armistice. Linking the republic to defeat and the Treaty of Versailles undermined its legitimacy from the start.

questions.stem: In Germany's Aims in the First World War (1961), Fritz Fischer argued that:
options: Britain deliberately provoked the war to destroy Germany as a naval rival
the war was caused by Serbia and Russia, with Germany acting defensively
Germany's leaders sought expansion and bore most blame for the war
all the great powers slid into war equally, with no one country to blame
questions.explanation: Fischer used government archives to show ambitious German war aims and continuity with later expansionism, provoking fierce debate in West Germany. His work challenged the comfortable post-war view that Germany had not been especially to blame.

questions.stem: After the defeat at Stalingrad, Joseph Goebbels gave his 'Total War' speech in Berlin in February 1943. Its purpose was to:
options: announce Germany's surrender on the Eastern Front and peace talks with Stalin
explain why the Nazi government would not ask women to work in industry
end rationing so that civilians would support the war after Stalingrad
rally the public behind full mobilisation of labour and resources for the war
questions.explanation: Goebbels demanded sacrifices from all Germans, including closing non-essential businesses and drawing more people into war work. The staged speech shows the regime trying to rebuild morale after a disaster it could not hide.

questions.stem: Albert Speer, appointed armaments minister in 1942, is associated with:
options: the Nazi youth movement as leader of the Hitler Youth
a big rise in arms output until 1944, despite Allied bombing
the planning of the Holocaust at the Wannsee Conference in 1942
the decision to invade the Soviet Union in June 1941
questions.explanation: Speer rationalised war industry and production rose sharply, partly through the exploitation of forced and slave labour. His post-war claims of ignorance about Nazi crimes have since been widely challenged by historians.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the German war economy's use of labour during the Second World War?
options: Millions of foreign forced labourers and prisoners worked in Germany
German women were conscripted into factories earlier than in Britain
Industry relied almost entirely on German volunteers until 1945
Foreign workers were paid equal wages and given equal rights
questions.explanation: By 1944 millions of foreign civilians, prisoners of war and camp inmates worked in German farms and factories, many in brutal conditions. Nazi ideology made the regime reluctant to mobilise German women as fully as Britain did.

questions.stem: The White Rose resistance group, whose leaders Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed in February 1943, was made up of:
options: army officers who plotted to assassinate Hitler
Communist workers who sabotaged arms factories
Catholic bishops who preached against the war
Munich students who spread anti-Nazi leaflets
questions.explanation: The group wrote and spread leaflets condemning Nazi crimes and urging resistance. The Scholls were caught at the University of Munich and executed after trial by the People's Court. The army officers' plot came in July 1944.

questions.stem: On 20 July 1944, Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg:
options: led a Communist uprising in Berlin that was put down by the SS within hours
surrendered his army to the Allies in Normandy against Hitler's direct orders
assassinated Heinrich Himmler, leading to a struggle for control of the SS
left a bomb at Hitler's headquarters, but Hitler survived and the plot failed
questions.explanation: The bomb at the Wolf's Lair in East Prussia wounded Hitler but did not kill him, and the attempted takeover in Berlin failed. Thousands were arrested and many executed. The plot showed that some of the old elite had turned against Hitler, though late.

questions.stem: In August 1941 Bishop Clemens von Galen preached publicly against the killing of disabled people under the 'euthanasia' program. Which conclusion is best supported by what followed?
options: Public protest could make the regime change tactics, though killing continued
The regime abandoned the persecution of all minority groups because of church pressure
Open protest was impossible, since Galen was immediately arrested and executed
The program had never been official policy and was ended once Hitler learned of it
questions.explanation: Hitler officially halted the gassing program known as T4 in August 1941 to avoid conflict with the churches, but disabled people continued to be killed by other means. Galen was not arrested, as the regime feared making him a martyr.

questions.stem: After Germany's unconditional surrender in May 1945, the country was:
options: placed under a single Allied military government in Berlin
split into two states, East and West, within the first month
returned to self-government under an elected German chancellor
divided into four occupation zones, with Berlin also divided
questions.explanation: Britain, the USA, the USSR and France each controlled a zone, and Berlin, inside the Soviet zone, was divided into four sectors. Germans often call the moment of total defeat 'Zero Hour'. The two German states were founded only in 1949.

questions.stem: The Allied policy of denazification aimed to:
options: punish all German civilians collectively by deporting them to Allied countries
restore Nazi officials to their posts so that Germany could be governed
require all former Nazis to emigrate to the Soviet Union for re-education
remove Nazis from public life, using questionnaires and tribunals
questions.explanation: Millions of Germans filled in questionnaires and were classified by tribunals. The process became bogged down, and in the West many former Nazis returned to careers as the Cold War made rebuilding Germany a priority.

questions.stem: At the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg (1945-46):
options: German courts tried the guards of every concentration camp and sentenced every one of them to death
Hitler and Himmler were tried in absentia and sentenced to life imprisonment
the Allies tried German civilians who had voted for the Nazi Party in 1933
leading Nazis were tried for crimes against humanity and other crimes, and twelve got death sentences
questions.explanation: The trial of the major war criminals introduced charges of crimes against peace and crimes against humanity. It set precedents for later international justice. Hitler and Himmler had killed themselves before it began.

questions.stem: The Basic Law (Grundgesetz) adopted in May 1949 was the constitution of:
options: the Allied Control Council governing Germany
a reunified Germany in its 1937 borders
the Federal Republic of Germany
the German Democratic Republic
questions.explanation: The Basic Law created the Federal Republic, with its capital at Bonn and Konrad Adenauer as first chancellor. The GDR was founded in October 1949 under the Socialist Unity Party (SED).

questions.stem: The Basic Law included a 'constructive vote of no confidence', so that the Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor. This was designed mainly to avoid:
options: the election of a chancellor directly by the people, as in the Kaiser's time
rule by a military government, as under the Allied occupation after 1945
the unstable governments and deadlock that had weakened the Weimar Republic
the dominance of one party, as the SED came to dominate East Germany
questions.explanation: Weimar parties could unite to bring a government down without agreeing on a replacement. The Basic Law's designers also weakened the president, created a strong constitutional court and allowed bans on anti-democratic parties.

questions.stem: West Germany's rapid economic recovery in the 1950s, the 'economic miracle', is linked most closely to:
options: Soviet reparations paid to the western zones and the nationalisation of industry
a return to the Nazi Four-Year Plan under the direction of the same officials
the Hallstein Doctrine, which opened East German markets to Western exporters
currency reform, Marshall Plan aid and Ludwig Erhard's social market economy
questions.explanation: The 1948 currency reform and lifting of price controls, Marshall aid and Erhard's mix of free markets with social welfare all contributed. Later, labour shortages were met by recruiting guest workers, including from Turkey from 1961.

questions.stem: Konrad Adenauer, West German chancellor from 1949 to 1963, is best known for:
options: recognising the GDR and the Oder-Neisse line in treaties of 1970
binding West Germany to the West through NATO and European integration
negotiating reunification with the GDR on terms set by the Soviet Union
building the Berlin Wall to stop West Germans moving to the East
questions.explanation: Adenauer chose Western integration over a neutral, united Germany: the Federal Republic joined the European Coal and Steel Community, NATO (1955) and the European Economic Community (1957). Recognition of postwar borders came under Brandt.

questions.stem: The uprising in East Germany on 17 June 1953 began when:
options: soldiers of the East German army mutinied and occupied Berlin's centre
construction workers in East Berlin protested against higher work quotas
students in Leipzig demanded the reunification of Germany under Adenauer
farmers refused to join collective farms and burned state property
questions.explanation: The protest over raised work norms spread to hundreds of towns with demands for free elections. Soviet tanks crushed it. West Germany marked 17 June as a national holiday until reunification.

questions.stem: Historian Mary Fulbrook has described the GDR as a 'participatory dictatorship'. This interpretation stresses that:
options: many ordinary citizens took part in running the system as well as being controlled
the GDR was a genuine democracy because citizens voted in elections every few years
the Stasi was too weak to watch citizens, so the regime relied on Soviet troops alone
East Germans were free to leave and chose to stay because of full employment
questions.explanation: Fulbrook accepts that the SED ruled through repression and surveillance but argues that large numbers of people participated in its mass organisations and local bodies. The view complicates a simple picture of a population purely oppressed by the Stasi.

questions.stem: Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik, from 1969, aimed to:
options: rebuild the Wehrmacht so that West Germany could defend itself without NATO
expel guest workers and limit migration from Eastern European countries
improve relations with the GDR and Eastern Europe through treaties
force the Soviet Union to withdraw from East Germany by threatening sanctions
questions.explanation: Brandt's government signed treaties with Moscow and Warsaw (1970), accepting existing borders, and the Basic Treaty with the GDR (1972). Both German states joined the United Nations in 1973.

questions.stem: In December 1970 Willy Brandt knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. The gesture is significant because it:
options: announced West Germany's withdrawal from NATO and the European Community
celebrated the Red Army's liberation of Warsaw at the end of the war
acknowledged German responsibility for Nazi crimes, in Poland and beyond
marked the signing of the treaty that reunified East and West Germany
questions.explanation: The unplanned gesture, made while in Warsaw to sign a treaty recognising Poland's western border, became a symbol of a Germany facing its past. Brandt received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971.

questions.stem: The Frankfurt Auschwitz trials of 1963-65 are significant in West German history because they:
options: were the first trials of Nazi leaders, held by the four Allied powers
ended all prosecutions of former Nazis in the Federal Republic
convicted Adolf Eichmann and sentenced him to death in Germany
brought detailed evidence of the camp before the German public
questions.explanation: West German prosecutors tried former SS personnel from Auschwitz, and survivor testimony was widely reported. The trials helped push Germans towards confronting the Nazi past, a process called Vergangenheitsbewältigung. Eichmann was tried in Israel.

questions.stem: In autumn 1989, mass demonstrations in Leipzig challenged the East German regime. They became known for the slogan:
options: 'Peace, land and bread'
'Bread and work for all'
'We are the people'
'Workers of the world, unite'
questions.explanation: The Monday demonstrations grew from prayer meetings at the Nikolai Church. On 9 October 1989 about 70,000 people marched and the security forces did not intervene, a turning point. Later the slogan shifted to 'We are one people', a call for unity.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why the East German regime could not survive the crisis of 1989?
options: The SED won free elections in 1989 but chose to dissolve the state
The United Nations ordered the GDR to merge with the Federal Republic
Gorbachev would not send Soviet troops to save it as citizens fled
West Germany invaded the GDR after Honecker refused to open the border
questions.explanation: Without Soviet backing, the SED faced mass emigration through Hungary and Czechoslovakia and growing protests at home. Honecker was replaced in October, and the regime's improvised opening of the border on 9 November accelerated its collapse.

questions.stem: Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990 when:
options: the GDR's states joined the Federal Republic under its Basic Law
the two states merged to form a new country with a new constitution
the Soviet Union handed the GDR to the Western Allies to govern
a referendum in both states elected a new all-German parliament
questions.explanation: After free East German elections in March 1990 and monetary union in July, the eastern states acceded to the Federal Republic. The Two Plus Four Treaty, signed in September by the two German states and the four wartime Allies, settled the international issues.

questions.stem: In the first years after reunification, many East Germans experienced:
options: high unemployment as state firms were sold or closed
a sharp fall in living standards below those under Honecker
the loss of their right to vote in national elections
forced resettlement to the western states for retraining
questions.explanation: The Treuhand agency privatised or shut thousands of uncompetitive enterprises, and unemployment in the east soared. Resentment and 'Ostalgie', nostalgia for aspects of GDR life, showed that unity was harder than many had expected.

questions.stem: Angela Merkel, chancellor from 2005 to 2021, is significant in Germany's post-unification history as:
options: the last head of the GDR before it joined the Federal Republic
the first woman, and first person raised in the GDR, to lead united Germany
the chancellor who negotiated reunification with Gorbachev in 1990
the founder of the Alternative for Germany party in the early 2000s, as a protest
questions.explanation: Merkel grew up in the GDR and led governments through the euro crisis and the 2015 refugee crisis, when Germany admitted very large numbers of asylum seekers. Helmut Kohl was chancellor at reunification.

questions.stem: The 'Sonderweg' (special path) thesis argued that Nazism grew from Germany's distinctive history, such as the lack of a successful liberal revolution. Historians David Blackbourn and Geoff Eley criticised it mainly by arguing that:
options: Germany had a successful liberal revolution in 1848 that created democracy
Nazism was caused entirely by the Treaty of Versailles and the Depression
the Sonderweg thesis ignored Germany's long history of peaceful democracy
Germany's development was not so different from other European countries
questions.explanation: In The Peculiarities of German History (1984) they questioned the idea of a 'normal' Western path from which Germany deviated, pointing to Germany's modern economy and active middle-class society. The debate shows how historians explain the Nazi era by placing it in a longer story.

questions.stem: A historian studying East German society uses Stasi files on ordinary citizens. Which is the main caution needed?
options: Very few Stasi files survive, so they cannot be used for any research
They record only the views of senior SED leaders, not ordinary people
They were written by and for the secret police, reflecting its suspicions
They were written after 1990 by West Germans who never lived in the GDR
questions.explanation: The files are a rich source, opened to researchers and the people watched after 1990, but informers and officers had reasons to exaggerate or distort. Historians cross-check them with interviews, diaries and other records.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that West Germany's break with the Nazi past was incomplete in the 1950s?
options: The Basic Law guaranteed human dignity and allowed anti-democratic parties to be banned
West Germany paid reparations to Israel under an agreement signed in 1952
The Federal Republic joined NATO and the European Economic Community
Many former Nazi officials, judges and teachers returned to their careers
questions.explanation: As denazification ended, large numbers of former Nazi Party members returned to public service, and few were prosecuted until the 1960s. The other options show a deliberate break with the past or a turn to the West.
